summary: For ages 8–9 (UK Year 4 Sound; conceptual bridge to NGSS 4-PS4-1): children find the pattern that, for the same sound-maker and listening position, a bigger vibration (larger SIZE) usually makes a LOUDER sound, while keeping this distinct from pitch (how fast the object vibrates). The central difficulty is dissociating volume from pitch, so activities make the vibration visible, change only the striking/plucking force in a fair test, have children articulate the pattern in both directions, and contrast a louder-same-pitch change against a higher-same-volume change. 'Amplitude' is seeded informally as 'the size of the vibration' to pre-load later wave work. Work here is Tier A (concrete/observational): an articulated, demonstrated pattern from the child's own manipulation, not a quantitative amplitude measure.
misconceptions: Confusing volume with pitch — thinking a louder sound is automatically higher, or that turning something 'up' changes the note; the two must be dissociated explicitly.
Believing hitting/plucking HARDER makes a HIGHER pitch (rather than a louder sound of the same pitch).
Thinking volume is a property of the object alone rather than of how strongly it is made to vibrate.
Assuming the sound's loudness at the ear equals the vibration's strength regardless of distance (distance-fading is a separate, later idea).
Treating 'amplitude' as the height/size of the object instead of the size of its back-and-forth movement.

activities.title: Rice on the drum: hit harder, watch and listen
steps: Scatter a few grains of rice or salt on a drum skin (or stretched clingfilm/foil over a bowl).
Predict out loud: when I hit harder, will the rice jump higher or lower, and will the sound be higher, lower, louder, or quieter? Say WHY before hitting.
Hit the drum gently, then hit the SAME drum much harder, keeping everything else the same.
Describe what you saw (how high the rice jumped) and what you heard (how loud, and whether the note sounded higher or lower).
State the pattern in your own words in BOTH directions: 'harder hit → bigger vibration → louder sound' and 'gentler hit → smaller vibration → quieter sound.'
activities.insight: For the same drum and listening conditions, a larger vibration usually produces a louder sound. Compare pitch separately: striking harder may mainly change loudness, but do not treat an observed pitch change as impossible.

activities.title: Twanged ruler and plucked band: arc width and blur
steps: Hold a ruler firmly over the edge of a desk so part of it overhangs, keeping the overhang length FIXED.
Twang it gently, then twang it hard; watch how wide the arc is and listen to how loud it is.
Do the same with a plucked elastic band or guitar string: pluck softly, then strongly, and watch how much more widely the string blurs.

Say what stayed roughly the same and what changed. With moderate plucks and fixed length and tension, the note may stay approximately the same while the swing and loudness change; report any differences actually observed.
Describe the observed swing and loudness. With a fixed ruler or band and moderate plucks, a wider swing usually sounds louder while the pitch may stay roughly the same; report any pitch change too.
activities.insight: With the same ruler or band and the same listening position, a wider swing (a bigger vibration) usually sounds louder. The overhang length of the ruler, and the length and tension of the band or string, mainly set pitch, so these are held fixed.

activities.title: Two separate controls: compare amplitude and frequency
steps: Use a controlled wave model and prepared audio comparisons to distinguish vibration size from vibration frequency. For the loudness comparison, use the same note and listener position; for the pitch comparison, use sounds matched roughly in perceived loudness.
Keep frequency fixed in the model and increase amplitude: observe the wider vibration trace and hear the same note played more loudly at a comfortable level.

Change frequency in the model while keeping the trace amplitude fixed. Compare higher and lower notes using audio matched roughly for loudness; notice that higher pitch does not necessarily mean louder sound.

Explain which feature changed in each comparison: the size of the vibration or the number of vibrations each second. Do not use whisper-versus-shout throat feeling as a measure of vibration amplitude.

State the rules separately: for the same sound and listening conditions, a larger vibration amplitude usually gives a louder sound; more vibrations each second gives a higher pitch. Real instrument changes can affect both, so check what is actually held constant.
activities.insight: Volume and pitch are two different qualities that can be changed separately in a controlled model: for the same note and listening conditions, loudness mainly depends on the SIZE of the vibration, while pitch depends on how FAST it vibrates. Changing loudness need not change the note, and changing the note need not change loudness.

activities.title: Sort and predict: which change makes it louder?
steps: Sort prepared controlled examples into changes in loudness, changes in pitch, both, or depends on conditions. For real shortening or tightening, describe what was measured or heard rather than assuming only one quality changes.
For a 'predict which will be louder' prompt, choose and justify your answer in terms of which produces the bigger vibration BEFORE testing it.

Watch out for a tricky option that is HIGHER in pitch but is NOT actually louder — a change that only raises the note can tempt you into calling it 'louder'; decide carefully whether each change affects volume, pitch, or neither.

For pictures representing the same frequency, sound-maker and listening conditions, predict the order from smaller to larger vibration amplitude, then compare the corresponding sounds. State what was held constant.
Check your predictions against a real sound-maker where possible.
activities.insight: The learner can discriminate changes that affect volume from those that affect pitch, and can justify loudness predictions by the size of the vibration — and recognise that a higher note is not automatically louder.

activities.title: Talk it through with a drummer
steps: After hands-on work, explain to a questioner (real partner or an in-role 'percussionist/sound engineer') what happens to the note and the loudness when you hit softer.
Answer the probe: 'If I hit softer, does the NOTE change or just the loudness?' and justify with what you saw and heard.
Respond when the questioner pushes back on a wrong answer, revising your explanation.
Name 'amplitude' as 'the size of the vibration' and use it correctly in a sentence.
activities.insight: Children consolidate and articulate the volume–vibration-size pattern and the volume/pitch distinction in their own words, catching any remaining confusion.

checkQuestion: You hit a drum gently, then hit the SAME drum much harder. How is the second sound different — is it higher, lower, louder, or quieter — and what is different about how the drum skin is moving? Explain.
checkAnswer: The harder hit is LOUDER (not higher). Hitting harder makes the drum skin vibrate with BIGGER movements, and the bigger/stronger the vibration, the louder the sound. The pitch (how high or low) stays about the same — only the loudness changed.
